In May, reports began circulating that Tencent's Weixin Group (WXG) would abolish its team-leader system. Unlike previous officially announced reorganizations, this change proceeded quietly, without a company-wide email or internal announcement.

Several current and former Tencent employees told China Entrepreneur that multiple WXG departments were piloting a project-owner system. Previously, Tencent organized work into teams of as few as three to five people or more than ten, with a team leader allocating work. Several teams formed a business department or studio led by a director. Under the adjustment, these fixed groupings are broken up: employees assemble around projects, and permanent line-management roles such as team leader and director are replaced by project owners.

One employee said the main purpose was to strengthen the focus on business results and performance while reducing the management responsibilities attached to established positions. "Team leaders and directors used to hold fixed positions. Once they become project owners, they can move up or down and must take responsibility for their own project's profits and losses."
Similar changes are taking place in Tencent's Hunyuan large-model team.

An employee said that after Yao Shunyu became Tencent's AI business leader, he simplified reporting from "front-line employee—team leader—director" to three levels: "front-line R&D staff—project-area owner—Yao Shunyu," making management follow the business.

Behind this transformation is Tencent's determination to break down internal fiefdoms, bring younger people into leadership, and reinvigorate the organization. Tencent may also be trying to simplify its structure to address anxiety over moving more slowly than competitors in AI.

At the time, Tencent was facing a cool reception in capital markets. Its share price had fallen from a January 2026 high of HK$633 to HK$455.20 on May 20, erasing nearly one-third of its market value, or roughly HK$1.5 trillion. The falling share price had also reduced compensation for many Tencent employees, unsettling staff.

Tencent released its first-quarter 2026 results on May 13. Asked at the earnings briefing whether Tencent was falling behind in AI, Pony Ma replied: "A year ago, we thought we had boarded the boat, only to discover that it was leaking. Now it feels as though we have managed to stand on it, but still cannot sit down. We hope it can move faster."

According to China Entrepreneur, Tencent has made considerable efforts to reshape its organization in recent years, with Pony Ma speaking about it repeatedly both internally and publicly. Yet the actual effects still fall short of market expectations. One employee put it bluntly: "Tencent doesn't have too many team leaders; it has too many fiefdoms."
Bringing in younger leaders is not easy

What exactly distinguishes a project-owner system from a team-leader system? The question has been raised frequently inside Tencent, without a common answer. "It is old wine in a new bottle. The leaders are still the former team leaders and directors, and newcomers still find it hard to move up," one Tencent employee said.

Employees more often perceive the adjustment as a reshuffling of titles rather than a genuine transfer of authority. This sense of unchanged substance contrasts sharply with Pony Ma's long-standing ambition to bring younger people into management.

Around 2019, Pony Ma asked a pointed question at an internal meeting: "Among Tencent's one or two thousand director-level managers, how many are under 30? The answer is fewer than ten." The figure prompted Tencent to decide to adjust middle management to keep pace with business changes. Ma also made a remark that was subsequently widely quoted: "You may have done nothing wrong; in the end, the only problem is that you have become too old."

But around 2020, changes such as working from home unexpectedly created growth opportunities for internet and gaming businesses. Tencent's workforce expanded rapidly, interrupting the effort to bring younger people into leadership.

In 2023, Pony Ma revisited the issue in a company-wide letter. He called for "putting the people in the best form on the field," explaining: "Motivation can be stimulated, behavior can be managed, and results can be measured." His comments were also interpreted as a sign that senior management had developed structural concerns about Tencent's businesses and was determined to reform the organization.

A former employee told China Entrepreneur that from then on, business groups such as PCG began making limited changes from a team-leader system to a project system. "For a while, management even hinted that newly promoted team leaders should preferably be under 30."

Besides changing reporting levels, the project system placed greater weight on responsibility for profits and losses. The same employee said that after the reform, employees' year-end bonuses would also be directly tied to the profitability of their projects.
The organization still needs to work together

The reform aimed at "eliminating team leaders" has prompted two views inside Tencent. Some consider it a key step toward greater agility; others believe it treats symptoms rather than causes and cannot resolve deeper problems.

At the annual employee meeting in January 2026, Pony Ma again said that during the preceding year Tencent had "substantially improved the composition of its AI workforce and brought in more younger, AI-native talent."

But one technical employee said Tencent's AI efforts remained fragmented. WXG, TEG (Technology Engineering Group), and CSIG (Cloud and Smart Industries Group) each had their own large-model teams, with insufficient unified strategic design and resource coordination. Despite controlling the company's largest pool of user traffic and carrying hopes for a breakthrough, Weixin had not yet produced a benchmark AI application.
Indeed, a major reason WXG was at the forefront of this reform was the innovation pressure it faced from the group.

At the May 13 earnings briefing, Martin Lau emphasized: "Within the Weixin ecosystem, we have an opportunity to create a very distinctive artificial intelligence, encompassing the social graph, communication, communities, and the content systems represented by Official Accounts and Channels."

As Weixin needs to integrate with AI and create new products, the work and resources required have increased sharply. China Entrepreneur learned that at Tencent's 2026 annual meeting, a senior Weixin executive publicly expressed a desire to train its own large model and asked the group for more GPU support.
While Weixin was under pressure on several fronts, WXG's independence from the group and tendency to work in isolation also generated internal dissatisfaction.

An employee said Weixin preferred building its own platforms or models to using the company's CodeBuddy tool. One reason was that using the company's own models required internal chargebacks: "Open-source models can be set up and deployed independently anyway, so alternatives are readily available." Another was that "the capabilities of the company's own models may not meet Weixin's high standards."
A similar pattern of internal fiefdoms was present in the Yuanbao team. In January 2025, Yuanbao was transferred from TEG to CSIG and placed under Wu Zurong, formerly the head of Tencent Meeting.

China Entrepreneur learned that Yuanbao's product organization had recruited many employees with ByteDance backgrounds over the past year. At the same time, Wu Zurong brought former Tencent Meeting colleagues into Yuanbao. The two sides often disagreed in their thinking. Someone close to Tencent said plainly: "The two sides frequently clash."

Tencent also hoped organizational reform would pass pressure down through the organization and help resolve these problems. However, two experienced industry figures offered China Entrepreneur similar judgments: Tencent's continuing difficulty in finding its footing originated at the top, with "insufficient attention and resource commitment to AI."

"Although Tencent has increased GPU purchases, Tencent Cloud's approach remains an extension of its existing cloud business. It is still a follower and has not established a leading advantage. In high-value user-traffic settings such as social networking, gaming, and content-driven e-commerce, Tencent has also not demonstrated a strong commitment to AI innovation and deployment. The integration of technology and business remains superficial," an industry figure said.
Compensation surges while the share price remains weak
This organizational reform, centered on removing fixed team-leader roles, is fundamentally an attempt by Tencent to find a way forward under multiple pressures.

Since the beginning of the year, Tencent Holdings' share price had trended downward amid volatility. The loss of nearly one-third of its market value posed a serious challenge for a company that relies heavily on equity incentives to retain talent.

Tencent's 2025 financial report showed share-based compensation expense of RMB31.859 billion, up 36% year on year, while total compensation costs reached RMB130.7 billion, up 15.9%. The 36% increase in share-based compensation was much higher than the 15.9% increase in overall compensation costs.

Tencent employees said many key contributors had been promised substantial equity incentives to attract AI talent, a common industry practice. ByteDance had likewise introduced dedicated "Doubao shares" to reward key personnel.

Capital markets had entered a cycle centered on the AI narrative, however, and Tencent's AI business fell short of expectations, prompting investors to lower their outlook. The weak share price then affected key employees' income and morale, casting a shadow over further recruitment.

Tencent invested heavily in the AI red-packet promotions around that year's Spring Festival. Its financial results showed first-quarter capital expenditure of RMB31.936 billion, up 16% year on year and 63% quarter on quarter. User retention, however, was difficult to regard as satisfactory. QuestMobile's 2026 China Mobile Internet Spring Report showed that in March 2026, Doubao had 345 million monthly active users, ranking first among AI-native apps, while Yuanbao had only 57.34 million and ranked fourth.

Rumors recently circulated in the industry that Yao Shunyu would leave. Although Tencent quickly denied them, the rumors reflected deeper market concerns about the stability of Tencent's AI strategy and its ability to retain key talent.

Pony Ma's statement—"Now it feels as though we have managed to stand on it, but still cannot sit down. We hope it can move faster"—also put direct pressure on the technical teams to deliver results as soon as possible.

When business progress stalls, organizational adjustment often becomes an early option. But simplifying the organization alone may not help Tencent quickly escape a "death spiral." What Tencent most needs is to bring forward AI products that can genuinely convince the market.
